items.readable_text:
Content:
A subgraph of a graph [MATH: G] is a graph whose vertices form a subset of the vertices of [MATH: G] and whose edges form a subset of the edges of [MATH: G.] In other words, a subgraph is a part of the original graph.

Content:
Notice that a subgraph must be a valid graph, i.e., if it includes an edge, it must also include both of its endpoint vertices from the original graph.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] below and two of its valid subgraphs, [MATH: G_1] and [MATH: G_2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0c4fbc86f23ecca7c44bd67decb28980]

Content:
Please note that although the graph [MATH: G_2=(V_2, E_2)] may not seem like a valid subgraph of [MATH: G=(V, E),] it actually is.

Content:
- The set of vertices of [MATH: G_2] is [MATH: V_2=\{v_1, v_2, v_3\},] which is clearly a subset of [MATH: V=\{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4\}.]
- The set of edges of [MATH: G_2] is [MATH: E_2=\{v_1- v_2, v_2-v_2, v_2 - v_3\},] and each of these edges also belongs to [MATH: E.]

Content:

sections.normalized_html:
The complement of a simple (no loops or multiple edges) graph [MATH: G] is the simple graph [MATH: \overline{G}] with the same vertex set as in the graph [MATH: G,] and an edge belongs to [MATH: \overline{G}] if and only if it does not belong to [MATH: G.]

So, we start by drawing all the vertices of our initial graph.

Now, we add edges that were not included in the initial graph. There are [MATH: v_1 - v_2] and [MATH: v_2-v_3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A subgraph of a graph [MATH: G] is a graph whose vertices form a subset of the vertices of [MATH: G] and whose edges form a subset of the edges of [MATH: G.] In other words, a subgraph is a part of the original graph.

Content:
Notice that a subgraph must be a valid graph, i.e., if it includes an edge, it must also include both of its endpoint vertices from the original graph.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] below and two of its valid subgraphs, [MATH: G_1] and [MATH: G_2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0c4fbc86f23ecca7c44bd67decb28980]

Content:
Please note that although the graph [MATH: G_2=(V_2, E_2)] may not seem like a valid subgraph of [MATH: G=(V, E),] it actually is.

Content:
- The set of vertices of [MATH: G_2] is [MATH: V_2=\{v_1, v_2, v_3\},] which is clearly a subset of [MATH: V=\{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4\}.]
- The set of edges of [MATH: G_2] is [MATH: E_2=\{v_1- v_2, v_2-v_2, v_2 - v_3\},] and each of these edges also belongs to [MATH: E.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Complement of a Graph

Content:
The complement (or edge-complement) of a simple (no loops or multiple edges) graph [MATH: G] is the simple graph [MATH: \overline{G}] that has the same vertex set as [MATH: G] but whose edge set includes only the edges that are not present in [MATH: G.]

Content:
In other words, to construct the complement of a graph, we add edges where they are missing in [MATH: G] and remove edges where they exist in [MATH: G].

Content:
